geometryObservations: Chase geometry is built from four primitives on a ≈5 u lane: partial-width holes (steer or jump, G-S1-a), full-width pits (must jump, G-S2-a), half-width fences (must steer, O-S2-b) and mines (avoid; they cost distance, O-S1-a). Every hazard asks for a lateral move or a jump, never a stop.
The boulder (≈4 u) nearly fills the ≈5 u lane, so it can never be sidestepped or let past; the geometry's only exit is forward (O-ALL-a).
Lethality is split by kind: fences and pits kill on contact, mines only launch and slow — they are delayed-lethal, paid in distance to the pursuer (F2 POINT3).
Alternation is the rhythm: holes cut in from alternating edges (G-S2-b), fences alternate L-R-L (O-S2-b, O-S3-a, O-S4-c) — the player reads a left–right cadence rather than individual hazards.
Combined hazards dictate the landing: two quick pits then a fence, so land left (G-S3-a); a pit with a fence on the landing's left, so jump on the right (G-S4-c); a Nitro lane then a pit (G-S3-b).
Lane width narrows late: a lengthwise trench leaves ≈1.5–2 u (G-S3-c) and the Nitros hug one edge — narrow lanes appear only after the wide-lane lessons.
Shelters split the run into four short chases: every roofed room stops the boulder, holds the checkpoint and releases a fresh boulder when the player leaves (P-S1-c, P-S2-a, P-S4-a).
Chase endings are geometric: bridge 1 is destroyed behind the player (O-S3-b), bridge 2 drops the boulder (P-S3-b), and the final chase ends only at the goal.
Speed pads appear only after the first-half chase (P-S3-d) and in the final one, and one pair is aimed at a mine (P-S4-c): the tool that buys distance is also a steering test.

The final chase is a rhythm of slab islands separated by full-width pits (P-S4-b) with mines and fences standing on the islands — a jump every slab, the longest no-stop sequence in the stage (J-S4-a).
There are no creatures and no mask: the pursuer and the geometry carry all of the danger, and distance is the only safety.

The bonus is the opposite register — a calm side-scroll with precision geometry (steel sandwich walkway, crate bridge, TNT column) — a rest between chases that also rehearses the side spin needed at the final fences.
geometryTransfer: Chase lane: a 6 m-wide lane with a `zone` dir N (run at the camera) and a `stone` with `chase: true` and radius ≈2.3 m — a 4.6 m ball leaves ≤1.5 m beside it, so it cannot be sidestepped; a `wall` on one side and an open drop on the other.

Hazard cadence at 9 m/s on foot: partial-width `pit`s 2–2.5 m long covering 60–70 % of the lane, alternating sides every 10–15 m (≈1.1–1.7 s); full-width `pit`s ≈2 m with ≥3 m landing strips. The 5.6 m running jump clears them with margin, so the difficulty is the cadence, not the length.
Mines as non-lethal costs: 1 m `tumblezone` triggers (they knock the rider down without killing, and the chase stone gains) in singles, pairs and one row of three across the lane as a hurdle.

Landing-dictating combos: a 2 m `pit` followed by a half-width lethal barrier (a Nitro row or a lethal collider) on the left half of its landing; two 2 m pits with a 2.5 m strip between them and a barrier after, so the second jump must be aimed.

Shelters: a roofed room with a `checkpoint` every 120–200 m; end each chase stone's travel at the room entrance and start a new one when the player leaves; end the first-half chase on a bridge where the stone's travel stops and drops away.

On the board the same lane at cruise (12 m/s) cuts reaction time by a quarter and the full ollie (≈6.6 m) makes 2 m pits trivial, so add hazards rather than gap length; put one `speedpad` pair (board boost) before the hardest segment, aimed at a hazard 8–10 m ahead, so steering after the boost is mandatory.
